src.q: Codeine phosphate 30mg Tablets BP

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Acute moderate pain not relieved by paracetamol or ibuprofen alone (patients over 12 years); dry or painful cough; diarrhoea.

src.q: Codeine is indicated in patients older than 12 years of age for the treatment of acute moderate pain which is not considered to be relieved by other analgesics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen (alone).
Dry or painful cough Diarrhoea

items.t: MHRA: in children, only for acute moderate pain in those older than 12 years, and only if paracetamol or ibuprofen alone do not work.

src.q: Codeine should only be used to relieve acute moderate pain in children older than 12 years and only if it cannot be relieved by other painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen

items.t: Pain (adults): lowest effective dose for the shortest time, up to 4 times a day at intervals of not less than 6 hours; maximum 240 mg codeine per day; limit to 3 days and review if no effective relief. The SmPCs accessed give no separate adult mg-per-dose figure for pain.

src.q: Adults Codeine should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest period of time. The dose may be taken, up to 4 times a day at intervals of not less than 6 hours. Maximum daily dose of codeine should not exceed 240mg.
The duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days

items.t: Dry or painful cough (adults): 15-30 mg 3-4 times daily.

src.q: For dry or painful cough Adults: 15-30mg 3-4 times daily.

items.t: Diarrhoea (adults): 30 mg three to four times daily (range 15-60 mg).

src.q: Diarrhoea Adults: 30mg three to four times daily (range 15-60mg)

items.t: Elderly: reduce the dose.

src.q: Elderly Dosage should be reduced in elderly patients.

items.t: Agree a treatment plan and end-of-treatment plan before starting; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: When a patient no longer requires therapy with codeine, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Under 12 years: should not be used (risk of opioid toxicity).

src.q: Codeine should not be used in children below the age of 12 years because of the risk of opioid toxicity

items.t: 12-18 years, pain: 30-60 mg every 6 hours when necessary (0.5-1 mg/kg), maximum 240 mg daily; limit to 3 days (MHRA).

src.q: The recommended codeine dose for children 12 years and older should be 30-60mg every 6 hours when necessary up to a maximum dose of codeine of 240 mg daily. The dose is based on the body weight (0.5-1mg/kg).
Duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days

items.t: Cough: contraindicated under 12 years; not recommended at 12-18 years with compromised respiratory function. Diarrhoea: not recommended in children.

src.q: Codeine is contraindicated in children below the age of 12 years for the symptomatic treatment of cough
Codeine is not recommended for use in children aged 12 years to 18 years with compromised respiratory function for the symptomatic treatment of cough

items.t: Contraindicated in all under-18s having tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. Not recommended where breathing may be compromised.

src.q: In all paediatric patients (0-18 years of age) who undergo tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome
Codeine is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Acute respiratory depression; hypersensitivity to codeine or other opioid analgesics; obstructive airways disease; liver disease; severe hepatic dysfunction; acute alcoholism.

src.q: Acute respiratory depression, hypersensitivity to codeine or other opioid analgesics or to any of the excipients, obstructive airways disease, liver disease, severe hepatic dysfunction, acute alcoholism.

items.t: Where inhibition of peristalsis should be avoided: risk of paralytic ileus, abdominal distension, acute ulcerative colitis, antibiotic-associated colitis, diarrhoea caused by poisoning.

src.q: Codeine is also contraindicated in conditions where inhibition of peristalsis is to be avoided, where there is a risk of paralytic ileus, where abdominal distension develops

items.t: Breastfeeding; known CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers; under-18s after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea.

src.q: In women during breastfeeding (see section 4.6) In patients for whom it is known they are CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers

items.t: Also in section 4.3: use should be avoided in raised intracranial pressure or head injury (treated here as a contraindication); should not be given to comatose patients.

src.q: Use should be avoided in patients with raised intracranial pressure or head injury
Codeine should not be given to comatose patients.

items.t: Caution or reduced dose in asthma and decreased respiratory reserve; avoid during an acute asthma attack.

src.q: Use with caution or in reduced doses in asthma and decreased respiratory reserve, avoid use during an acute asthma attack

items.t: Caution or reduced dose: elderly or debilitated, hypotension, hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy, adrenocortical insufficiency, inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, urethral stricture, shock, convulsive disorders, myasthenia gravis.

src.q: in patients with hypotension, hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy, adrenocortical insufficiency, inflammatory or obstructive bowel disorders, urethral stricture, shock, convulsive disorders, myasthenia gravis

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop with repeated use; use with caution with a history of drug abuse; discontinue gradually.

src.q: Repeated use of codeine can lead to OUD.
Use with caution in those with a history of drug abuse.

items.t: CYP2D6 ultra-rapid or extensive metabolisers: increased risk of opioid toxicity even at usual doses.

src.q: if the patient is an extensive or ultra-rapid metaboliser there is an increased risk of developing side effects of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Caution in pancreatitis and biliary tract disease (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction). Another UK SmPC: opioid analgesics should be avoided in biliary tract disorders, or used with an antispasmodic.

src.q: codeine has to be administered with caution in patients with pancreatitis and diseases of the biliary tract
Opioid analgesics should be avoided in patients with biliary tract disorders or used in conjunction with an antispasmodic.

items.t: MAOIs: avoid codeine during and for 2 weeks after MAOI treatment.

src.q: the use of codeine should be avoided while the patient is taking MAOIs and for 2 weeks after MAOI discontinuation

items.t: Contains lactose (galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine as it contains lactose.

items.t: Anxiolytics and hypnotics: enhanced sedative effect. MHRA: co-prescribe benzodiazepines and opioids only if no alternative, at lowest doses for shortest time, with close monitoring.

src.q: Anxiolytics and hypnotics: enhanced sedative effect.
if a decision is made to co-prescribe, use the lowest doses possible for the shortest duration of time and carefully monitor patients for signs of respiratory depression

items.t: Alcohol, anaesthetics, sedating antihistamines, antipsychotics, sodium oxybate: increased CNS/respiratory depression and hypotension.

src.q: Alcohol: the hypotensive, sedative and respiratory depressive effects of alcohol may be enhanced.
Antipsychotics: enhanced sedative and hypotensive effect.

items.t: Gabapentin or pregabalin: respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

src.q: The concomitant use of codeine with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death

items.t: Sertraline (sertraline SmPC): serotonin syndrome / NMS risk is increased with opioids; caution and monitor for symptoms.

src.q: and with opioids. Patients should be monitored for the emergence of signs and symptoms of SS or NMS syndrome
Caution is also advised with opioids

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel presumably because of slowed gastric emptying. The clinical relevance is unknown.
Consider the use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in acute coronary syndrome patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists.

items.t: Renal impairment: avoid or reduce the dose (no numeric threshold stated).

src.q: It should be avoided or the dose reduced in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

items.t: Liver disease and severe hepatic dysfunction are listed as contraindications; section 4.4 also says avoid or reduce the dose in hepatic impairment.

src.q: obstructive airways disease, liver disease, severe hepatic dysfunction, acute alcoholism
It should be avoided or the dose reduced in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

items.t: SmPC: caution, especially in the first trimester (possible association with respiratory and cardiac malformations). Regular use may cause neonatal withdrawal; use in labour may depress neonatal breathing.

src.q: As with all medications caution should be exercised during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester. A possible association with respiratory and cardiac malformations has been reported following first trimester exposure to codeine.
Administration during labour may depress respiration in the neonate

items.t: BUMPS: take in pregnancy only if recommended by a doctor; most studies do not show harm; use near delivery can cause neonatal withdrawal and breathing problems.

src.q: Codeine should only be taken during pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
Codeine used around the time of delivery can affect your baby after birth.

items.t: SPS: codeine may be used where paracetamol has not been effective; most data do not suggest increased malformation risk.

src.q: The weak opioid codeine may be used where paracetamol has not been effective.

items.t: Contraindicated in breastfeeding (SmPC 4.3). Section 4.6 wording: not recommended; if opioid toxicity develops in mother or infant, stop all codeine and use non-opioid analgesics; consider naloxone in severe cases.

src.q: In women during breastfeeding (see section 4.6)
Administration to nursing women is not recommended as codeine may be secreted in breast milk and may cause respiratory depression in the infant.

items.t: MHRA: codeine should not be used by breastfeeding mothers.

src.q: Codeine should not be used by breastfeeding mothers because it can pass to the baby through breast milk and potentially cause harm

items.t: SPS: avoid. If a few doses are taken accidentally, stop codeine and monitor the infant (sedation, slow breathing/apnoea, poor feeding); get medical advice for significant effects.

src.q: Codeine should not be used during breastfeeding.
the mother should be advised to stop taking codeine and the infant monitored for side effects such as sedation, slowed breathing rate/apnoea

items.t: Sexual dysfunction, erectile dysfunction and decreased libido are listed adverse effects (frequency not stated).

src.q: Reproductive system and breast disorders: sexual dysfunction, erectile dysfunction, decreased potency. Decreased libido.

items.t: Most common: drowsiness, nausea, vomiting and confusion (tolerance develops with long-term use). Also constipation, dry mouth, dizziness, headache (frequency not tabulated).

src.q: Tolerance and some of the most common side effects - drowsiness, nausea, and vomiting, and confusion - generally develops with long term use.
Gastrointestinal disorders: nausea, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, stomach cramps, pancreatitis.

items.t: Respiratory depression (large doses) and opioid toxicity, especially in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers; may be life-threatening.

src.q: Large doses produce respiratory depression.
In severe cases this may include symptoms of circulatory and respiratory depression, which may be life-threatening and very rarely fatal.

items.t: Addiction and drug withdrawal syndrome; taper to stop.

src.q: Regular prolonged use of codeine is known to lead to addiction and tolerance.

items.t: Convulsions (especially in infants and children), pancreatitis, hypersensitivity syndrome.

src.q: convulsions (especially in infants and children)

items.t: Review benefit-risk regularly; monitor for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. early repeat requests).

src.q: The risk-benefit of continued use should be assessed regularly by the prescriber.
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: Pain: if no effective relief within 3 days, seek medical review.

src.q: The duration of treatment should be limited to 3 days and if no effective pain relief is achieved the patients/carers should be advised to seek the views of a physician.

items.t: Oral.

src.q: 4.2 Posology and method of administration Oral route

items.t: Can cause drowsiness and blurred or double vision; do not drive or use machines if affected. Alcohol effects are enhanced.

src.q: Codeine produces sedation and may also cause changes in vision, including blurred or double vision. If affected, patients should not drive or operate machinery.

items.t: MHRA: explain risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; do not stop suddenly after long-term use.

src.q: discuss with patients that prolonged use of opioids may lead to drug dependence and addiction, even at therapeutic doses

items.t: Children 12-18: parents should know the signs of morphine toxicity and stop codeine and seek help at once if they occur.

src.q: Symptoms of codeine toxicity include: reduced levels of consciousness; lack of appetite; somnolence; constipation; respiratory depression; 'pin-point' pupils; or nausea and vomiting
